sections.1: Job and his household

notes: “A man of integrity” describes Job’s soundness of character. It does not claim that he has never done anything wrong.
“His day” may identify a customary feast day or a birthday; the Hebrew does not settle this.
The Hebrew uses “bless” here as a euphemism for cursing, as also in 1:11 and 2:5, 9. Verse 21 uses blessing in its ordinary sense.
“The accuser” translates a title with the definite article. The scene does not itself supply the later biography associated with Satan. “Sons of God” names the heavenly assembly.
“Fire of God” is the messenger’s description of the disaster.
“Return there” places the mother’s womb beside death and the earth. The image is retained without making its physical geography explicit.
vocabulary: To regard God with reverence and live accordingly.
An image of protective enclosure; Job later uses enclosure as an image of confinement.

sections.1: A second challenge

notes: The words “without cause” explicitly disconnect Job’s suffering from a prior offense that would justify it. The divine speech also retains the accuser’s role in inciting the attack.
“Curse” translates the same euphemistic use of “bless” found in chapter 1.
The narrator says Job did not sin “with his lips.” The qualification is part of the text.
vocabulary: The wholeness of character that Job continues to hold to.
The friends first come to grieve with Job and offer consolation.

sections.1: Job curses the day of his birth
sections.20: Why give light to the suffering?

notes: The Hebrew expression rendered “deep shadow” can also evoke the shadow of death.
The pointed Hebrew can mean finding no joy among the days; another reading concerns not being joined to their number.
Leviathan evokes a formidable creature of chaos. Job calls on imagined powers capable of undoing the day of his birth.
The “ruined places” are difficult: rebuilding ruins or constructing monuments that become ruins are possible senses.
The phrase can mean sighing in place of bread or sighing before eating.
vocabulary: The first opening of morning light.
The protection pictured in 1:10 becomes confinement in Job’s lament.

sections.1: Eliphaz: Can anyone be right before God?

notes: The first line names the lion’s roar without a complete verb; the draft supplies “falls silent” from the surrounding image of broken power.
The word for “spirit” can also mean wind or breath. The account remains Eliphaz’s report of his experience.
The question can ask whether a mortal is righteous before God or more righteous than God.
The comparison with a moth is compressed. Being crushed more easily than a moth is one reading; other readings picture destruction by or like a moth.
vocabulary: Human bodies pictured as fragile dwellings founded in dust.

sections.1: Eliphaz: Seek God

notes: The rare word rendered “the thirsty” has also been understood as robbers.
“Sparks” renders “sons of flame,” an expression that may also evoke birds or the name Resheph. The upward-flying image is retained.
“Almighty” is the traditional rendering of Shaddai; the title’s precise derivation is uncertain.
Six troubles followed by seven is an ascending number pattern, not a limit on the troubles named.
The rare expression for vigor pictures maturity at death; it does not supply a numerical age.
vocabulary: A poetic picture of harmony with the land, followed by peace with wild animals.

sections.1: Job: My grief has weight
sections.24: Show me where I went wrong

notes: The substance paired with tasteless food is uncertain: egg white and the juice of a plant such as mallow are possibilities.
The verb for exulting or taking comfort amid pain is uncommon. Job’s refusal to deny the Holy One’s words is retained.
The draft takes the sufferer as the one who may abandon reverence for the Almighty. Another reading accuses the friend who withholds loyalty of abandoning that reverence.
The Hebrew may describe caravans turning aside or the channels of streams running away. The caravan reading continues the travelers’ search for water.

The written and read forms differ: the written form can yield “you have become nothing,” while the read form means “to it/him.” “That is what you have become to me” relates the friends to the failed stream; the wording remains uncertain.
vocabulary: Loyal care expected within a relationship, even when the sufferer’s faith is shaken.

sections.1: Job: Days without hope
sections.7: Remember how brief my life is

notes: The word for hope can also mean a thread or cord, echoing the weaver’s shuttle.
Sea and the sea monster evoke threatening powers held within bounds. Job asks why he requires such guarding.
The difficult comparison literally sets strangling and death against “my bones,” the exhausted bodily life he is enduring.
The pinned Hebrew says Job has become a burden “to myself.” The draft preserves that wording.
vocabulary: The realm of the dead; the word does not by itself identify a place of punishment.
An image for even a moment’s respite.

sections.1: Bildad: God does not twist justice

notes: Bildad attributes the children’s death to their sin. This is his accusation, not a statement by the narrator.
The wording describing confidence as fragile or cut off is rare. The spider’s house makes its insecurity vivid.
The roots are pictured seeing or reaching toward a house of stones. The ancient image is retained.
“Joy” can be heard ironically: the plant’s apparent flourishing ends in replacement by another.
vocabulary: Here, a person estranged from or disregarding God; Bildad applies the category within his argument.

sections.1: Job: Who can contend with God?
sections.25: There is no arbiter between us

notes: Bear, Orion, and Pleiades are conventional identifications of the Hebrew star names; the exact ancient groupings are uncertain.
Rahab here is a poetic chaos figure, not the woman in Joshua.
The Hebrew reads “Who can summon me?” The first person is retained. It can be heard as a challenge voiced by God; other readings make Job the speaker of the question, or render it with “him.”
The subject that would declare Job twisted can be his own mouth or God. The line preserves the pressure of a defense that turns against him.
The material of the swift boats is uncertain; reed boats is a common understanding.
The closing phrase is exceptionally compressed, literally something like “not so am I with myself.” The draft understands Job as unable to speak freely under present conditions.
vocabulary: A name associated with the defeat of chaotic power.
Someone able to bring both parties together and hear their dispute. No specific figure is identified.

sections.1: Job: Tell me why you accuse me
sections.18: Why did you bring me out of the womb?

notes: Milk curdling into cheese is an ancient bodily image of formation in the womb, retained as poetry.
The final words are read as an appeal, “look at my affliction,” rather than absorbed into a description of misery.
The read forms address God with imperatives; the written forms can continue speaking of him in the third person.
vocabulary: God’s attention to Job’s life becomes the basis of Job’s bewilderment at his suffering.

sections.1: Zophar: If only God would speak

notes: The phrases about wisdom’s double depth and God’s treatment of guilt are difficult. The draft understands Zophar to claim that Job is receiving less than his guilt deserves.
The last question can mean that God sees without investigation or that wrongdoing cannot escape his attention.
The wild donkey becoming human can be an impossible comparison that mocks an empty-headed person’s supposed wisdom. Another reading allows the possibility of learning.
The rare word rendered as darkness can concern gloom or failing light.
The verb may mean looking around securely or digging about before settling down.
vocabulary: The realm of the dead, paired with the heights of heaven to describe what exceeds human reach.

sections.1: Job: I have understanding too
sections.13: Strength and wisdom belong to God

notes: The opening is difficult. The draft reads contempt for another’s disaster; a discarded torch is another proposed image.
The final line can picture carrying one’s god in one’s hand or receiving abundance from God’s hand. The draft retains the unsettling former image.
The divine name LORD appears here in the dialogue and is preserved.
The draft reads the bonds as those imposed by kings, then pictures the kings themselves bound. Another understanding concerns removing the kings’ belts or signs of office.
vocabulary: The image turns the authority of rulers into their own captivity.

sections.1: Job: I want to argue my case with God

notes: Taking flesh in the teeth and life in the hand pictures mortal risk. The question is retained rather than converted into a calm statement.

The read form means “for him”; the written form means “not.” The draft follows the read form: Job waits for God even under threat of death. Following the written form yields “I have no hope.” In either case Job insists on arguing his conduct to God’s face.
The relation between a successful challenge, silence, and death is compressed. The draft keeps the conditional force.
Marking or tracing the soles of Job’s feet may picture surveillance or the marks of confinement.
The Hebrew shifts to “he,” understood here as a wasting human being, not as God decaying.
vocabulary: Job challenges the use of dishonest advocacy in God’s defense.
Job frames his appeal in the language of a legal hearing.

sections.1: Job: A mortal’s few days
sections.13: If only you would hide me

notes: The question concerns cleanness arising from uncleanness. No developed account of inherited guilt is supplied.
The question about living again remains a question within Job’s wish; it is not turned into a settled declaration.

The draft continues the hoped-for situation: God would count Job’s steps without keeping watch over sin. These lines can instead be heard as a return to present scrutiny and guilt being preserved in a sealed bag.
Pain and mourning continue in the closing image. The poem does not resolve exactly how this relates to death or the dead.
vocabulary: The appointed period of waiting is pictured as compulsory service.

sections.1: Eliphaz: Your own mouth condemns you

notes: The verb describing the eyes is rare; flashing or signaling with them are possible senses.
Eliphaz invokes ancestral authority and the absence of foreigners. The claim belongs to his argument.
The thickened body pictures wealth and security in the description of the wicked man.
The last phrase concerns possessions or their spread; its precise wording is uncertain.
vocabulary: Eliphaz accuses Job of using calculated, evasive speech.

sections.1: Job: Miserable comforters

notes: Job says he could strengthen them with his mouth. This can be heard as sincere consolation or as an ironic echo of their empty comfort.
The speech moves from “he” to direct address, “you.” The draft preserves the shift.
The word can name archers or arrows. The images of split kidneys and spilled gall remain graphic.
The first phrase is difficult: it can describe the friends as mockers or evoke interpreters or advocates. The draft follows the mocking-friends reading.
The heavenly witness is not named. The plea for someone to argue a human being’s case before God is left within Job’s own speech.
vocabulary: An image of strength or dignity, now thrust into the dust.
Uncovered blood calls attention to a wrong still demanding an answer.

sections.1: Job: Who will stand surety for me?

notes: Job asks God for security in a dispute with God. The tension is retained.
This compact saying concerns betrayal of companions for a share or reward, followed by harm to the betrayer’s children. Its precise wording is uncertain.
“Desires” renders an expression literally concerning the possessions of the heart.
The grammar of the final question, including who goes down and rests together, is difficult. The draft follows Job’s hope down to the bars of Sheol without resolving every pronoun.
vocabulary: A pledge or guarantor securing an obligation.
The realm of the dead imagined as a place of confinement.

sections.1: Bildad: The wicked man’s light goes out
sections.14: Driven to the king of terrors

notes: Bildad uses plural forms of “you,” although Job is his immediate opponent.
The word rendered “unclean” is rare and has also been understood as dull or stupid.
The line may describe famished strength or disaster hungry for its victim.
The first line can describe something not belonging to the man occupying his tent. The following sulfur image is retained without silently supplying a different Hebrew text.
The paired expressions can refer to west and east or to later and earlier generations. The draft follows the geographic reading.
vocabulary: A personification of a powerful, deadly affliction.
A poetic ruler of death’s terrors; the text does not identify a historical king.

sections.1: Job: How long will you crush me?
sections.23: I know that my redeemer lives

notes: “My own family” renders “sons of my womb,” an unusual expression for close kin. It can also be understood as Job’s own children, which creates a tension with the opening narrative.
The expression “skin of my teeth” is obscure. Its vivid image of barely surviving is preserved.

The redeemer is a defender or vindicator, but the poem does not name this figure. Standing at last upon the dust and seeing God “from my flesh” permit different understandings of timing and bodily life. “From” can be understood as from within or apart from the flesh. The draft does not settle these questions through later doctrine.
The pinned Hebrew says “in me,” not “in him.” The change of person is retained in Job’s report of his opponents’ accusation.
“Not a stranger” can contrast Job’s own seeing with another person’s, or describe seeing God no longer as a stranger. The draft follows the first reading.
The final expression is difficult but concerns judgment. The warning retains the relation between wrath, offenses, and the sword.
vocabulary: A person who acts to reclaim, protect, or vindicate another; here a hoped-for defender of Job’s case.
The Hebrew names the kidneys, a bodily image for deep feeling and longing.

sections.1: Zophar: The triumph of the wicked is brief

notes: The relation between spirit and understanding is compressed. Zophar presents his reply as arising from his own understanding.
The first line can concern children seeking favor from the poor or making restitution to them. The second line names the man’s own hands returning wealth.
The wording about gain and exchange is difficult; the central claim is that the man cannot enjoy the wealth he has acquired.
The last word can be related to food or eating; other interpretations concern fighting. The draft pictures wrath raining down as the man’s food.
vocabulary: The bitter bodily fluid, here part of a graphic image of a weapon piercing the body.

sections.1: Job: Listen to what I am saying
sections.7: Why do the wicked live on?
sections.17: How often does disaster reach them?

notes: The questions continue across both verses. Job challenges the claim that the wicked regularly meet these disasters.
“You say” makes an inferred objection explicit; the Hebrew does not mark the quotation with those words. Job answers that the offender himself should experience the consequences.
The word rendered “vessels” is uncertain; proposed senses include milk pails or parts of the body such as breasts or loins. The parallel line describes well-nourished bones.
The wording can mean being spared on the day of disaster or reserved for that day. The draft follows the former in keeping with Job’s argument that the wicked escape the fate his friends predict.
The grave is watched, but the Hebrew does not specify who keeps watch.
vocabulary: The realm of the dead; Job contrasts an easy descent there with a life of suffering.

sections.1: Eliphaz: Is not your wrongdoing great?

notes: The alleged offenses are accusations made by Eliphaz. The narrator has not established that Job committed them.
The opening “or” and the relation of darkness to seeing are abrupt in the Hebrew.
The pinned text asks what the Almighty could do “to them,” not “to us.” The draft preserves the shift out of the preceding direct speech.
The term rendered “adversaries” is uncommon and uncertain.
The short exclamation can call for lifting the fallen or refer to pride. The draft follows the appeal to lift them up.
The opening word is rare. Read as a negative, it gives “one who is not innocent”; an alternative connects it with an island or region of the innocent.
vocabulary: A source of prized gold; its location is uncertain.

sections.1: Job: If only I knew where to find him

notes: The Hebrew can describe Job’s complaint as defiant or bitter. It reads “my hand,” though many render “his hand.” The draft retains Job’s hand and the difficult comparison with his groaning.
Forward, back, left, and right can also be understood as east, west, north, and south.
The comparison can refer to allotted food or to Job’s own prescribed course.
“One” can emphasize God’s single purpose or his unique, unopposed standing.
The final sentence is difficult. The draft understands Job as not silenced by darkness; another reading concerns not being cut off before darkness came.
vocabulary: Job imagines arranging his arguments for a hearing.
Refining supplies an image for being tested and emerging with integrity.

sections.1: Job: Why are no days of judgment set?
sections.13: Those who rebel against the light

notes: The appointed times are understood as times for judgment from the surrounding question about God’s days.
The second line does not explicitly repeat a child as the object taken in pledge. The draft retains that restraint.
“Between their walls” can also be understood as among their rows, in the setting of pressing oil.
The final clause can mean God does not charge anyone with wrongdoing; another reading takes it as his not attending to the cry.

These lines are difficult to connect with the surrounding argument. They have been read as Job’s own description, a curse or wish, or a quotation of an opponent. The draft preserves their received order and attribution to Job without adding a new speaker.
The subject is understood here as God drawing away the mighty. Alternatives concern God prolonging their life or a powerful person acting by his own strength.
vocabulary: Food for animals; the poor glean what they can from another’s fields.

sections.1: Bildad: Who can be pure before God?

notes: Maggot and worm are Bildad’s images for human frailty and uncleanness within his argument. They are not detached statements by the narrator.

sections.1: Job: Whom have you helped?

notes: The “shades” are the dead, named by the Hebrew term Rephaim.
Abaddon means destruction and here names the realm of death. The passage does not identify the figure named Abaddon in Revelation.
The earth suspended over nothing is a poetic image of divine power. It is not recast as a modern scientific account.
The word can refer to a throne or to the full moon. The draft follows the throne reading.
The verb can describe stirring the sea or bringing it to rest. The draft follows the latter alongside the shattering of Rahab.
The fleeing serpent belongs to the poem’s imagery of cosmic conflict.
The draft follows the read form’s plural “ways” or mighty deeds. These remain only the outskirts of what can be known.
vocabulary: A poetic name for chaotic power subdued by God.
What humans hear is only a faint trace of divine power.
